The convergence of a sequence of polynomials B_n(x) to a function f(x) on [0, 1] does not necessarily imply uniform convergence.

To see this, consider the sequence of polynomials B_n(x) = x^n. This sequence converges pointwise to the function f(x) = 0 on [0, 1). However, it does not converge uniformly.

The reason is that the sequence B_n(x) = x^n does not satisfy the Cauchy criterion for uniform convergence. In fact, for any ε > 0, there exists an N such that for all n, m > N, |B_n(x) - B_m(x)| ≥ ε for some x in [0, 1).

For example, let ε = 1/2. Then for any N, there exists an x in [0, 1) such that |x^n - x^m| ≥ 1/2. This is because the sequence x^n is not uniformly bounded on [0, 1), and therefore cannot satisfy the Cauchy criterion for uniform convergence.

In general, if a sequence of polynomials B_n(x) converges pointwise to a function f(x) on [0, 1], it may not converge uniformly if the sequence is not uniformly bounded or if the convergence is not uniform on a subinterval of [0, 1].

In summary, pointwise convergence of a sequence of polynomials B_n(x) to a function f(x) on [0, 1] does not necessarily imply uniform convergence.
